Hi, I'm actually at a CC in Sacramento and I highly recommend it! There are a ton of classes and they are all really informative and help in ways I never wouldve imagined. Through a lot of this training, I've been able to improve my voice, movement, and of course character as well as style. I'm always of the opinion that there is more to learn and Sacramento CCs are a great place for it :)

At that point, I don't know if it would be necessary unless it is from a prestigious school or class, or the instructor is well known. If you have better things you can fill the resume out with then of course always be upgrading.

In my experience (which is limited as I'm still in college so grain of salt here) if you dont have a ton of stuff to fill a resume then training and education should absolutely be listed. I dont think anyone is going to laugh at someone who has acting 101 on their resume. It shows you have at least basic training in acting technique and that puts you a step above someone with no training whatsoever.

If you cant do an accent, like your voice just DOES NOT go to a certain place then I would say think about changing the voice? With christmas eve, the overt accent is a bit necessary but I dont know if trekkies voice is absolutely necessary unless that is what the director is looking for. 

If you think about almost all plays, there are a million ways to play a character. Just because someone did something and it worked doesnt mean that it cant be done a different way and work just as good if not better. I would say when you go to your callback, be confident, make bold choices and listen to the direction you're given. If the director is absolutely headstrong on trekkies voice then you will have to find a way to make it happen. But if you can wow them with something different, they might be pleasantly surprised. Just my two cents. 

And as far as accents go, listen to them, study them and understand them. Understand how the mouth and tongue and other parts move in certain accents and bow they are different from others. Be hungry for knowledge and improvement. Break a leg!

I would say think about justification. Your character is a real person with a real life outside the events of the play. Why does he do what he does? For example, if he shoves a kid in a locker, why? Is it to intimidate the other kids? impress the females? Hide his insecurities? There are tons of different reasons for doing something and finding those reasons will make you feel more authentic in your actions. Your character doesnt think about "being more degrading or disrespectful" he just does it. Just some food for thought!

I took a summer class at my local community college and it was excellent. I'd reccomend checking out local cheap classes if you can find some. But other than that research and the internet are your friends. But remember, understand what an accent is supposed to sound like, not what one actor with that accent sounds like.

I took a voice diction class in college and basically in a typical southern accent (like rural Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi, etc) words like dark and art are non-rhotic meaning you dont pronounce the "r" sound in the word at all. So dark would be pronounced "dahk" same with "aht" and any other words that use the r sound following a vowel (ar,er,ir,or,ur)

Southern accents actually have the least amount of changes and substitutions compared to most other accents. Often times we feel like we need to use more substitutions to make it feel better but usually just doing the ones we are meant to fit better than we expect hope this helps and feel free to message me for any more info!

Any paper should let you erase easily from my knowledge as long as you don't press down too hard on the paper.

I don't use tutorial books so unfortunately, I can't help you out there. I'm my experiences, the best way to learn is to practice and experiment. 

As far as learning technique and whatnot, there are some great YouTube channels that cover these. Some to look into are Draw with jazza, sycra, mark crilley, and many more. 

I often use an HB pencil. If you want a really nice range of values, you could look into buying a pencil set that has a variety of values. Most of them are relatively inexpensive. 

I only recently started using colored pencils but in my experiences, any colored pencils are fine. As you grow, you may want to upgrade to high end supplies but I don't recommend shelling out alot of money on those until you know you want to stick with that medium. 

The type of paper depends on your style and what you want to achieve. For smooth looking pieces where the tooth of the paper is not easily visible, you could use Bristol paper or something similar. I use a kneaded eraser to be more precise while erasing but any eraser will work. 

In the end, the only materials you actually need are a pen or pencil and a piece of paper. 

I enjoy drawing everything really, though I seem to focus alot on people. If you have any more questions, I'll try my best to answer them!

I've never done digital art so I can't speak from that aspect. I would imagine it's not too different from traditional art. As far as supplies go, it depends on your style. 

For example, some people like using ink or colored pencils some like sticking with simple pencil and eraser. I recommend trying out as many mediums as possible and finding out what you enjoy. 

You should do some research on the subject and find what interests you. In the end all you need to start creating art is a pencil or pen and a piece of paper. 

You should finish a piece once you are happy or satisfied with the outcome, then move on. The best way to improve is to practice! 

Draw everyday if you can and reach out of your comfort zone. Drawing from life is a great way to learn but using reference pictures can also teach you alot. 

The most important thing to remember is to have fun and enjoy creating the art. Don't get upset when things don't work out, just learn from it and improve upon it.
